**Service Name:** Shopify Terms of Service

**Summary:**

These Terms of Service outline the rules and agreements between you (the merchant/ user) and Shopify (the company). The main goal is to govern your relationship with Shopify and describe how its products and services work.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** These terms apply to all services and products described on Shopify's official terms page.
* **Content and License:** You own the content in your store, but Shopify can use it to improve and train its AI/ML systems as long as you've set up your account correctly and it's allowed by law.
* **Privacy:** Your personal data will be collected and processed in accordance with Shopify's Privacy Policy, which is available on their website.
* **Dispute Resolution:** In case of a dispute, you'll need to go through binding arbitration instead of taking it to court. This means you'll resolve the issue privately instead of going to public court. However, you have 30 days to opt-out of this requirement when creating a new account.
* **Termination:** Either party (you or Shopify) can terminate the agreement at any time, following the conditions outlined in this document.

**Clauses to Note:**

* **Use of Content:** Be aware that Shopify may use your store content to train its AI/ML systems. While it's stated that this usage is at the store level, ensure that you understand how your content is being used and that you're comfortable with it.
* **Dispute Resolution:** The requirement for binding arbitration might be considered limiting, as it may be difficult or costly to participate in arbitration. Also, the 30-day opt-out window gives you some flexibility, but be aware of this restriction when creating a new account.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SHOPIFY TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Shopify and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions, clarified that merchant store content may be used to power AI features only at the merchant's store level (not for training shared models), and revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Shopify to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms .

**Service Name:** Wikimedia Terms of Use

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** These Terms of Service apply to your relationship with Wikipedia (the Wikimedia Foundation) and cover the products and services listed on their official terms page.
* **Content and License:** When you contribute to Wikipedia, you grant them permission to use your content to operate, improve, and train their artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy:** This policy cross-references the company's Privacy Policy, which explains what personal data they collect and how they process it.
* **Dispute Resolution:** In disputes, binding arbitration is required unless you opt-out within 30 days of creating a new account. Note: This clause may be harmful to the user if they don't read and act on the opt-out window, as it limits their right to take the dispute to court.

Additional Provisions:

* **Changes:** The policy has undergone a major rewrite since 2014, expanding on issues like account-security and dispute-resolution provisions.
* **Termination:** Either party can terminate the agreement under the conditions listed in the live document.
* **Contact:** If you have questions, consult the company's published legal contact information.

**Potential Red Flags:** 

* The **binding arbitration clause** (Dispute Resolution) might limit your access to court, if you don't carefully read the opt-out notice.
* The **Content and License** clause may be concerning for users who don't agree with how their contributions are used to train AI/ML systems.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — WIKIMEDIA TERMS OF USE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2014 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2014 version in the following ways: Effective June 7, 2023: first major rewrite since 2014. Added Universal Code of Conduct as binding, updated paid-contributions disclosure rules, modernized account-security and dispute-resolution provisions, and added explicit language covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use . The previous version is available at https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use/9_June_2014 .

- The content license has been expanded to include the creation of derivative works and advertising.
- Data retention periods after account deletion have been extended from 18 months to 36 months.
- The right to participate in class actions is no longer available in dispute resolution.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service were updated with some significant changes. Here's what's new:

* The content license has been expanded. Previously, it only allowed ChirpSocial to display your content (Term 2 in the old Terms). Now, ChirpSocial has a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from content you post, including for advertising (Term 2 in the new Terms). This new license is particularly broad and may not work in your favor if you're posting valuable or proprietary information.
* The data retention period has increased from 18 months to 36 months after account deletion (Term 3 in the new Terms). This means your account data will be kept for a longer period, potentially impacting you if you're concerned about your information being stored for a longer time.
* The arbitration clause has been updated (Term 4 in the new Terms). Now, you're waiving your right to participate in any class action, which may not be favorable if you're concerned about group disputes.

No new clauses explicitly state that you're at increased risk or that ChirpSocial has new rights to use or exploit your information. However, the changes mentioned above are worth paying attention to.

New or updated clauses to review carefully:

* Term 2 (new): expanded content license (may affect your proprietary content)
* Term 3 (new): extended data retention period (more time for your data to be stored)

Remember, continued use of the service constitutes acceptance of the updated Terms.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Returns are now store credit only, no longer a full refund.
- Time frame for finalizing sales after delivery has been reduced from 14 days to 7 days.
- Users in the EU may now opt-out of purchase history sharing, but users outside the EU may not.
- ShopFast Pay has been added as a new accepted payment method.
- The term "Standard shipping" has been changed to "Standard delivery".

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service say that several changes were made to the purchasing agreement.

One change affects your right to return items. Previously, items could be returned within 14 days for a full refund. The new Terms of Service indicate that items may be returned within 14 days, but **only for store credit**. This means you won't receive a full refund for purchases made under these Terms.

Another change has to do with the waiting period before a purchase is final. The new Terms of Service say that a sale is final 7 days after delivery, whereas previously, a sale was final 14 days after delivery.

Furthermore, the new Terms of Service make it clear that **users in the EU can now opt-out of having their purchase history shared with marketing partners**. However, users **outside the EU are still not eligible to opt-out**.

Additionally, the new Terms of Service include a new payment method called ShopFast Pay, which joins Visa, MasterCard, PayPal, and other existing payment methods.

Lastly, the term "Standard shipping" has been replaced with "Standard delivery" to better reflect the expected timeframe.

The only possible clauses to flag as potentially new risks involve:

* **Loss of full refund in case of returns**, as items are now only eligible for store credit.
* **Increased scrutiny on users outside the EU** who are still not allowed to opt-out of purchase history sharing.

- Google can now use uploaded content "to develop and improve its services, including its AI services," which wasn't the case before.
- Users are now prohibited from abusing, reverse-engineering, or extracting underlying models from Google's generative-AI features.
- The dispute-resolution and governing-law sections have been updated, but specific details are not provided in the given excerpts.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the key changes.

First, the Terms of Service have reorganized some clauses to make them clearer. But the main changes are in these areas:

* **Content usage**: Previously, Google was only allowed to host, reproduce, and display your uploaded content to operate the services. Now, they can also use it to "operate, develop, and improve its services, including its AI services". This is a broader license.
* **Generative AI limitations**: There's a new section that prohibits you from "abusing, reverse-engineering, or attempt[ing] to extract underlying models" from Google's generative-AI features. This means you can't try to figure out how their AI works in certain ways.
* **Dispute resolution**: The sections describing how disputes are handled have been updated. Unfortunately, the specifics of the changes are not included in this excerpt, so we can't say what exactly has changed.
* **Liability**: The warranty disclaimers and capped-liability language have been updated. However, again, the specifics are not provided.

One thing to keep in mind is that the Terms of Service say Google can use your content in various ways, including for AI development. It's always a good idea to review what you upload carefully. As for the generative AI limitations, if you were planning to try to reverse-engineer Google's AI, you should be aware that this is no longer allowed.

It's worth noting that the updates might not necessarily harm you, but they do change the terms under which you use Google's services.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The effective date of the Terms of Service has been updated from 2024 to 2025.
- The new Terms of Service now require users to understand what data is exportable, with a dedicated subsection explaining this.
- Clarification has been added that some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement.
- Some trial-period offers now require auto-renewal to be turned on, previously this was not explicitly stated.
- Xbox-related services now warn users that non-Microsoft third-party platforms may be tracking and sharing their data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's walk through the changes.

The effective date of the Terms of Service has been updated from 2024 to 2025. This means the agreement is now in effect for a newer year.

Regarding YOUR CONTENT, there's a new subsection explaining what data users can take with them when their service ends. This means you have more clarity on what data you can export or transfer to another service.

In the SUPPORT section, the Terms of Service now clarify that some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement. This means you should check the individual service's support terms for specific details.

In the PAYMENT section, there's a new provision stating that some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on. This means you might be auto-renewing a trial period without intending to, so be sure to check the service's settings.

Lastly, in the XBOX section, Microsoft has added language about non-Microsoft third-party platforms potentially tracking and sharing your data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles. This is something to be aware of if you use these platforms.

As for new clauses that may harm you, the added provision about auto-renewal in trial-period offers (PAYMENT section) is something to be aware of. You might need to be more proactive with your trial periods to ensure you're not accidentally charged.

There is no specific new clause that is detrimental to users as of now. However, future updates might impact users. Be sure to check the Terms of Service for any updates.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The Effective Date of the Terms of Service has changed from 2023 to 2024.
- The Moderation section now includes a link to a detailed external policy page.
- The XBOX section now includes information about third-party data tracking and sharing.
- The KIDS ON XBOX section clarifies limitations of family-settings features on third-party platforms.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's review the changes. 

The Effective Date of the Terms of Service has been changed to 2024. This indicates that the previous Terms of Service, which were effective in 2023, are now deprecated. The new Effective Date is not a content change, but rather a marker for when these Terms of Service started to be in effect.

One key change is to the Moderation section. Previously, the Terms of Service only described moderation rules in-text. Now, the section includes a link to an external Microsoft policy page that provides more detail on moderation and enforcement. This change allows for more comprehensive information but does not directly impact the usage of services.

Regarding Xbox, the new Terms of Service add a disclosure: third-party platforms that host Xbox titles may track and share user data, as defined by those platforms' terms. This change adds an important note about potential data sharing when using Xbox on third-party platforms.

Additionally, the KIDS ON XBOX section now clarifies that family settings may be limited when using Xbox on third-party platforms. This change may affect users who have set up family settings and expect those to be in effect across all platforms.

To summarize, new clauses and changes relevant to you are:

* **Third-party data tracking and sharing (XBOX):** Note that third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may share your data.
* **Limited family-settings features (KIDS ON XBOX):** Family settings may not be fully available on third-party platforms.

These changes might be worth reviewing if you have previously set up family settings or are concerned about third-party data tracking. If you have further questions, feel free to ask!

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- SCOPE: The document is now split into separate terms for consumer use and business/API use.
- ARBITRATION: The arbitration provider has changed from ADR Services to National Arbitration and Mediation.
- BATCH ARBITRATION: The procedures for batch arbitration have been revised.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and there are some significant changes. 

First, the document is now split into two separate sets of terms: one for consumer use and another for business and API use. This means that each group will have its own set of rules and guidelines.

Regarding arbitration, the process has changed. Previously, you would go to ADR Services for binding arbitration. Now, the arbitration provider is National Arbitration and Mediation, which also implies the use of binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court).

Another change is to the batch arbitration procedures. The Terms of Service now reflect how National Arbitration and Mediation handles these procedures, rather than ADR Services.

There are no new clauses here that specifically target you as a consumer.
source_tos:
1. SCOPE. Consumer Terms of Use are split off; a separate Business Terms covers API and Enterprise.
2. ARBITRATION. Arbitration provider changed from ADR Services to National Arbitration and Mediation.
3. BATCH ARBITRATION. Procedures revised to reflect how National Arbitration and Mediation handles batch arbitration.

- Consumer Terms of Use formally separated from Business Terms (API/Enterprise).

[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Continued use of binding arbitration as the dispute-resolution mechanism (provider changed, mechanism unchanged).
[CASE TYPE]
substantial

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The old agreement separated different business services into distinct agreements, but the new agreement combines them into a single unified Services Agreement.
- The old agreement's data-handling provisions varied by product, whereas the new agreement has unified provisions for all services.
- The old agreement did not explicitly confirm that business and API customer data is not used to train OpenAI's models by default; the new agreement does.
- The old agreement scattered service-level commitments across separate addenda, but the new agreement updates and consolidates them into one place.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service include several changes.

One of the main changes is that the Terms of Service now encompass a single unified Services Agreement, which previously covered different business services in distinct agreements.

Another significant change is that the data-handling provisions have been unified across all services. This means that you will no longer have to navigate varying data-handling policies for different business services.

The new Terms of Service explicitly confirm that business and API customer data is not used to train OpenAI's models by default. This is a positive change for you, as it provides clearer assurances about how your data will be handled.

The Terms of Service have also been updated to include consolidated service-level commitments (SLAs). Previously, these commitments were scattered across separate addenda, but now they are all in one place.

Regarding the indemnification language, the updated Terms of Service consolidate and update the wording. Since this is an update, I'll assume it's a clarifying change rather than a potential harm.

However, since we don't have the exact details of the new indemnification language, it's impossible to comment further on this.

4. SLAs. Service-level commitments updated and consolidated.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to better reflect our services and policies. Here's what changed:

The scope of the Terms of Service has been expanded to explicitly cover the Claude apps in addition to Claude.ai and Claude Pro. This means we now have more clearly defined what services are subject to these Terms.

We've also added more clarity on linking accounts created with employer-owned email domains. Now, we're required to give notice before linking these accounts, which should give users more control over their accounts.

The Acceptable Use Policy is now more strongly referenced, which means you'll want to review that policy to ensure you're complying with its terms. The previous version simply referenced a separate policy, so this change may require some extra attention.

Lastly, the dispute-resolution and governing-law sections have been updated, although the specific changes aren't detailed in the new Terms. This may affect how disputes are resolved in the event of a disagreement.

There don't appear to be any new clauses that would specifically harm users. However, be aware of the stronger reference to the Acceptable Use Policy, as non-compliance with that policy could still result in consequences. The change to provide notice before linking employer-domain accounts may also be a point of confusion, so make sure you're aware of the linking process.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version implies an agreement by use, while the NEW version explicitly states using Meta products is agreement to the Terms.
- In the NEW version, the Content License allows Meta to distribute and modify user content.
- The NEW version of CONTENT LICENSE also includes language about improving and operating services beyond just deletion of content.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service have several changes worth noting.

The way the Terms of Service say you agree to them has been altered: using Meta products is now considered acceptance of the Terms. This means that by using Meta products (like Facebook), you automatically agree to the Terms, even if you don't explicitly click "I agree."

Regarding content you upload to Meta Products, the updated Terms of Service add new language that allows Meta to distribute and modify your content. This is to help improve and operate services. This is a change from the previous version, which only allowed Meta to display content you posted.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service retain standard provisions related to binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) but the rest of the changes in this section are unchanged.

As for any potential harm, be aware that Meta now has the right to distribute and modify your uploaded content to operate and improve services. This might be of concern if you uploaded sensitive or private information. 

The updated language also emphasizes that the content license granted to Meta extends beyond just displaying and deleting content. Meta can use your content to enhance and manage its services.

To summarize, here are the main changes:

* Using Meta products is now considered agreement to the Terms.
* Meta is granted more rights to distribute and modify your uploaded content.
* The content license now allows Meta to use your content to improve services beyond just displaying it.

Let me walk you through the updates to the Instagram Terms of Service.

Previously, the policy was limited to a non-exclusive license to host and display content users post. Now, the worldwide non-exclusive license has been expanded to include distribution and modification of uploaded content.

This version **adds** a new clause about AI/ML processing of content across Meta Products like Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger. This means your content may be used for service operation and improvement on these platforms.

Finally, the updates make data-flow provisions across Meta Products more explicit and broadened.

As for any potential harm, be aware that:

* Your content may now be distributed, modified, and used for service improvement, which could raise concerns about ownership and control.
* The increased data sharing between Meta Products may compromise your privacy.

These points are subject to the Terms of Service, so it's essential to review them carefully. 

To put it simply, these changes grant Instagram more rights to your content and may increase data sharing across Meta Products. If you have any questions or concerns, it's always a good idea to carefully read through the Terms.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope of the Content License has been expanded to include using posts to train machine-learning and generative-AI models.
- Users are no longer able to opt out of having their content used for AI training in the in-product settings.
- The Terms of Service now allow broader data sharing with third parties, potentially without user consent.
- The scope of the Terms has been narrowed from covering Twitter services to covering only X services.

[NARRATIVE]
This version updates the Content License to allow posts to be used for training machine-learning and generative-AI models worldwide (a royalty-free license). This expands the original license, which only covered using, hosting, and displaying posts.

The AI Training clause has been updated: users can no longer opt out of having their content used for AI training in the in-product settings (this setting has been removed). In the previous version, users had this option.

The THIRD-PARTY DATA SHARING clause now allows for broader data sharing with third parties, potentially subject to a license. This is no longer limited to partner relationships as it was before.

Finally, the SCOPE of the Terms has narrowed: the new version only covers X services, whereas the previous version also covered Twitter services.

New clauses that may harm you include:
* Using posts to train machine-learning and generative-AI models without explicit user consent
* Broader data sharing with third parties, potentially without explicit user consent

4. SCOPE. Covers X services.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The company name has changed from TikTok Inc. to TikTok USDS.
- The content license now includes a stronger guarantee it will not be revoked.
- The license for AI model development has been specifically reaffirmed.
- The rules for AI-generated content have changed, with users now directly responsible for AI use.
- AI users are no longer allowed to remove watermarks or claim AI output is human-made.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. 

When it comes to the contracting party, the company name has been updated from TikTok Inc. to TikTok USDS. This is simply a change in the name, and it doesn't have any direct bearing on your use of the app.

The content license has gotten stronger. Previously, it was a worldwide royalty-free sublicensable license. Now, it's an irrevocable, royalty-free, sublicensable license, reaffirmed for machine-learning (ML) model development. The key addition here is that the license is now **irrevocable**, which means it can't be withdrawn by the company.

The age policy remains the same. Users under 13 still need to use the Under-13 Experience.

However, there are new rules for using AI (artificial intelligence). In the past, there were limited provisions related to AI. Now, there are specific rules:
* Any content generated by AI comes "as is" and may not be challenged.
* You are fully responsible for the inputs and outputs of the AI, which means you need to make sure you're using it correctly.
* You're no longer allowed to remove watermarks from AI-generated content.
* You can't claim that AI-generated content was created by a human.

It's worth noting that these new AI rules are quite restrictive and may have implications for users who rely on the technology.

- - The ability to monetize videos is no longer limited to YouTube Partner Program creators.
- - YouTube can now monetize videos from non-Partner creators.
- - Facial-recognition data cannot be collected from videos.
- - No-U.S. creators now have U.S. tax-withholding obligations when receiving payments.
- - The Terms now apply to users globally, rather than being region-specific.

The updated Terms of Service bring several changes to the existing policy. Here are the highlights:

* **Monetization**: Previously, only YouTube Partner Program creators could monetize their videos. However, the updated Terms of Service say that YouTube has the right to monetize most videos on the platform, including those of non-Partner creators. This means that non-Partner creators are now subject to YouTube's monetization policies.

* **Facial Recognition**: The updated Terms explicitly prohibit collecting facial-recognition data from videos. This is a new restriction that did not exist in the previous Terms.

* **Tax obligations**: Non-U.S. creators now have U.S. tax-withholding obligations when receiving payments. This is a new requirement that may affect non-U.S. creators.

* **Global scope**: The updated Terms now apply to users globally, rather than being region-specific. This means that the policy applies uniformly across all regions and countries.

As for potential harm, here are some points to note:

* Non-Partner creators are now subject to monetization policies that may restrict their ability to earn revenue from their videos.
* The prohibition on facial-recognition data collection may add additional requirements or restrictions for certain types of creators or content.
* Non-U.S. creators may be subject to U.S. tax-withholding obligations, which could result in reduced payment amounts or additional administrative requirements.
* The global scope of the Terms may expose creators to additional requirements or penalties based on local laws and regulations.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope of Adobe's access to user content has been clarified and limited to improve services and software.
- Adobe specifically states that it does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content.
- The language of the Terms has been rewritten to be clearer and in plain English.
- Adobe will now provide plain-English summaries of changes alongside new updates.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to clarify some key points. 

Firstly, Adobe previously only accessed user content for narrow service-operation purposes. The updated Terms now clarify that access is broader - Adobe is allowed access via 'automated and manual methods' to improve services and software. **However, this update occurs in the initial version that was put into effect in February 2024, which caused public backlash due to its potential breadth. So only versions after the June update are preferable**.

To address concerns, the June update specifically states that Adobe doesn't train generative-AI models on customer cloud content, which should alleviate some worries about AI training for users.

Another point is that the Terms have been rewritten in clearer, plain language, which should make them easier to understand.

Lastly, the updated Terms now include plain-English summaries of changes alongside the Terms of Service, which should provide clear explanations for when changes were made.

It's worth noting that the broad access clause in the February 2024 version has been criticized for potentially compromising user privacy. **However, as it has now been specifically clarified in the June version, the updated Terms may address these concerns by establishing clear guidelines for Adobe's access to user content**.

Overall, while there are some changes that may raise concerns, the updated Terms aim to be more transparent and user-friendly.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Zoom was previously allowed to use customer service-generated data to train AI/ML models without consent, but a March 2023 update now requires a broad license for this purpose.
- From March to August 2023, Zoom allowed the use of customer service-generated data for AI model training, but now customers must consent for AI model training.
- The customer content remains covered by customer-controlled use in both versions.
- No change was detected in relation to the use of telemetry and operational data or the retention periods.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated with some significant changes. 

Firstly, regarding Service-Generated Data, Zoom was previously allowed to use it to improve its services without any specific consent or license. Now, a broad license is required from you to permit Zoom to use your service-generated data to train AI/ML models.

In August 2023, Zoom amended the Terms in response to some backlash. The new version explicitly states that audio, video, and chat content are not used to train AI models without your consent.

• **AI model training with consent**: A new requirement is that customers must give explicit consent before their data can be used for AI model training.
• **AI model training without consent**: Zoom can use service-generated data without consent, but that's okay as long as it's for AI/ML model training, according to March 2023 update, but customer doesn't see any use or harm.
• **Customer content usage in March to August 2023**:  From March to August 2023, Zoom was allowed service-generated data for AI model training and that change didn't raise any red flags.

It's essential to note that the Terms of Service now explicitly state that customer audio, video, and chat content are not used to train AI models without consent. This change aims to give you more control over how your data is used.

• **Customer-controlled use**: Customer content remains subject to customer-controlled use in both versions.

When considering these changes, it's crucial to be aware of the implications of the broad license in service-generated data and AI model training. As long as the customer is aware of AI training consent changes, it seems that these updates primarily emphasize transparency and user control over their data.

3. CUSTOMER CONTENT. Customer audio/video/chat continues to be subject to customer-controlled use.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The Terms of Service now explicitly state that member content may be used for AI training.
- The AI training clause has been added, stating that member data and content may be used to train generative-AI models.
- A new opt-out toggle in Settings has been added, allowing members to choose whether their data and content can be used for AI training.
- The dispute-resolution provisions have been updated and now include language to waive class-action lawsuits.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service say that the updates aim to clarify how your data and content are used.

To start, let's go over the new **CONTENT LICENSE** clause. The baseline license is the same, but now it explicitly includes using your data for AI training. This means your posts, comments, and other content can be used to train artificial intelligence models. If you're not comfortable with this, we'll talk more about the opt-out toggle.

Another change is the introduction of **AI TRAINING**. This new clause explicitly states that your data and content may be used to train generative-AI models for LinkedIn features. This essentially uses your data to make the platform better, but it also means your input may be relied upon in creating AI outputs.

Regarding new clauses that may harm you:
* **AI TRAINING** gives the company permission to use your data and content in ways you might not fully agree with, depending on your understanding of AIs.
Regarding potential harm:
* The **DISPUTES** section now includes a class-action lawsuit waiver in the updated dispute-resolution provisions. This means if you sue the company, you'll have to go through binding arbitration instead of a court trial. The terms of arbitration may not be in your favor.
* While not necessarily "new harm," it's essential to note that the opt-out toggle for **AI TRAINING** may not be easy to find or understand without being prompted, so take some time to review the settings.

Overall, it seems most changes aim to clarify existing processes.

4. DISPUTES. Updated dispute-resolution provisions, including class-action waiver language.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Personal data shared with affiliates is now explicitly restricted to Microsoft and GitHub affiliates.
- Personal data may be used for AI/ML model development, a new purpose that was not previously disclosed.
- AI/ML model training is now an explicitly stated purpose for using personal data.
- Opt-out preferences now allow for more control over data protection, but it has a condition attached, where it "travels with the data," implying that opting out might not completely stop the use of all data.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service have included a few key changes. 

Firstly, the list of affiliates that can receive your personal data has been updated. Previously, your data could be shared with affiliates for limited operational purposes. However, now it is explicitly limited to Microsoft and GitHub affiliates.

Another significant change is the introduction of new processing purposes for your personal data. One of the new purposes is for the development of AI/ML models. This is a specific clause that wasn't present in the previous Terms of Service.

The previous Terms of Service didn't have an explicit statement about using personal data for AI/ML model training. However, this version adds an explicit purpose for using personal data for this reason.

There are now more user controls over your data through opt-outs. However, the opt-outs have a condition attached - they "travel with the data when shared with affiliates." This is a bit concerning, as it suggests that even if you opt out, there might not be complete protection from the use of your data.

Overall, I would suggest you be cautious with how your personal data is shared. Make sure to exercise your opt-out preferences and monitor your data closely to ensure it aligns with your comfort level.

4. OPT-OUTS. User opt-out preferences and enterprise data protections travel with the data when shared with affiliates.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The option to share an account across households is no longer tolerated, a paid sharing feature is introduced with additional fees for users outside the primary household.
- A defined 'Netflix Household' concept is introduced to clarify account grouping.
- A new extra-member fee will be applied for users outside the primary household under the paid sharing feature.
- The billing and cancellation provisions have been updated to reflect the extra-member fee.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over what changed in the updated Terms of Service.

First of all, the way account sharing is handled has changed. Previously, *account sharing across households was tolerated in practice*, but that's no longer the case. **Now, you're required to have paid sharing to add users outside of the primary household.**

Here's how it works: the *paid sharing feature requires the primary household plus paid additional members for users outside it*. This means that if you want to add people outside of your primary household, you'll need to pay extra for them.

There are also some changes related to billing and cancellation. *The billing and cancellation provisions have been updated to reflect the extra-member fee*. This means you should expect some changes in how your account is billed if you have users outside of your primary household.

I'd like to highlight a new clause that clarifies how accounts are organized: the Terms of Service now explicitly define a *'Netflix Household' concept*. This means that when you set up your account, you'll be working with this defined household.

One potential issue you might face is if you're currently allowing friends or family members to share your account without paying extra. Unfortunately, *the Terms of Service say that the primary household plus paid additional members for users outside it* are the only way to share accounts in the new policy. This might result in you losing access to users outside of your primary household without upgrading your plan. However, I can't say if this impacts you specifically without more information. 

Lastly, I want to mention that the Terms of Service do not discuss any plans to automatically remove users outside of your primary household in the future, or if there are any alternatives to paid sharing.

- Ads can now appear on 'no ads' / 'ad-free' tiers.
- Arbitration procedures have been expanded and may now apply to more cases.
- Effective dates for subscribers no longer remain the same across all users.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the updates to the Terms of Service.

**Ads:** Previously, the 'no ads' / 'ad-free' tiers were genuinely ad-free for streaming titles. Now, streaming titles may include ads even for subscribers on these tiers. This change means that you may still see ads on your ad-free subscription.

**Arbitration:** The Terms of Service now have expanded mass-arbitration procedures. This change may allow Disney+ to apply arbitration to a wider range of cases, potentially impacting how disputes are resolved. Arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) can be binding, meaning the outcome may be final and required to be followed.

**Effective Date:** The Terms of Service previously had a single effective date for all subscribers. Now, there are different effective dates for new and existing subscribers. This change may affect when the updated Terms of Service apply to your account.

The new clause about ads is likely to harm users who subscribe to the 'no ads' / 'ad-free' tiers and expect an ad-free experience. The updated arbitration procedure may also be unfavorable for users who prefer to resolve disputes in court rather than through a private arbitration process.

3. EFFECTIVE DATE. Different effective dates for new and existing subscribers.

- The dispute resolution and chargeback flow have been expanded.

The **seller protection criteria** have changed. Previously, the policy was standard seller-protection criteria, but now there are **revised seller-protection criteria**. This means that PayPal may have updated its evaluation process for protecting sellers in certain situations.

You should note that this change might affect how PayPal handles disputes involving sellers.

**Cross-border fees have new schedules**. Instead of existing fee schedules, there are now new fee schedules for cross-border transactions. This may impact your costs when making or receiving international payments.

Regarding **disputes**, the Terms of Service add an **expanded dispute-resolution and chargeback flow**. This likely includes new procedures for handling disputes, but the exact changes are not clear from the provided information. It is possible that this new flow may be more complex and time-consuming.

Finally, the handling of **cryptocurrency holdings** has been clarified. While the previous Terms of Service only had limited references to cryptocurrency, the current version provides more information. This could impact how PayPal handles your cryptocurrency balances.

It's essential to review the current Terms of Service to understand the full implications of these changes. If you're unsure about any aspect, I recommend consulting the updated document or seeking advice from a financial professional.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- ADVANCED DATA PROTECTION - Apple offers optional end-to-end encryption for additional iCloud data categories.
- ENCRYPTION ACCESS - Apple's access to stored content for legal/safety reasons is narrowed in cases where end-to-end encryption is in use.
- APPLE INTELLIGENCE - Apple now uses privacy-preserving cloud compute for AI-related services.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes. The Terms of Service have been updated in several areas.

**Encryption:**
Apple now offers **optional** end-to-end encryption for additional iCloud data categories under Advanced Data Protection. This means that if you choose to opt-in, your data will be encrypted in a way that only you can access it.

**Access:**
Apple's access to stored content for legal or safety reasons has been **narrowed** in cases where you've opted-in for end-to-end encryption. This is a good change for you, as your data will be more secure.

**AI:**
Apple is now using **privacy-preserving cloud compute** for its AI-related services. This means that your data is protected when Apple uses AI to process it.

As for any new clauses that may harm you, the Terms of Service now explicitly mention that Apple may access your data for legal or safety reasons, but only in specific, narrower cases where you haven't opted-in for end-to-end encryption. However, the protection offered by Advanced Data Protection is not mentioned as a requirement that Apple will make exceptions for.

There is no clause in the updated Terms of Service that inherently states you'll be harmed by the changes. However, with more data encryption options at the user's discretion, less risks could possibly be inferred by some users in regards to more data being under Apple's control. The actual risks you may face are based on multiple factors and the context they're in, so it's essential to analyze more than just the Terms of Service before making any conclusions.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The crowd-sourced services license has been expanded.
- A section on My AI and other generative-AI features has been added.
- The pre-arbitration waiting period has been increased from no specified period to 60 days.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service say that when it comes to content you upload, the standard license remains the same.

However, the updated Terms of Service have made some changes to how content contributed by others is handled. In the old version, there was limited language regarding the expansion of the license for crowd-sourced services. Now, this version adds an "Expanded user-content license for Live, Local, and other crowd-sourced services." (This new license affects how you use content contributed by others in these specific services.)

The updated Terms of Service also touch on how the platform uses AI. This version adds a whole new section about "My AI and other generative-AI features." This includes language about the features themselves but doesn't introduce anything explicitly harmful.

One significant change in the arbitration procedure is the introduction of a 60-day waiting period before binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court). The old version did not have a specified waiting period. This waiting period can delay your access to the dispute resolution process.

In summary, the key changes are:

* Expanded license for content contributed by others in certain services
* Additional provisions for AI features
* Increased waiting period for pre-arbitration procedure

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version had no clause regarding AI partner-sharing, but now the NEW version may share public Tumblr posts with AI partners for training.
- The OLD version had no opt-out option to prevent third-party sharing, but the NEW version includes a user-facing opt-out in Settings > Visibility.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service include some important changes. 

Regarding new clauses that may affect you: 

* There's a new clause regarding AI partners. Currently, in Settings > Visibility, you have an opt-out option called "Prevent third-party sharing" that might help you prevent Tumblr from sharing your content with these AI partners.
* Additionally, your public Tumblr posts may be shared with AI partners for their training, which is specified under the "AI PARTNERS" section.

Changes from the previous version include:

* The old version did not include any clause about AI-partner-sharing, whereas the current version may share public Tumblr posts with AI partners for training.
* The old version did not have an opt-out option, whereas the current version includes a user-facing opt-out in Settings > Visibility.

To keep in mind:

* When it comes to sharing your content with AI partners, you can opt-out in your settings, but once your public posts are shared, that content is out of your control.
* You may want to review your settings and decide whether or not to use the opt-out option.

The Terms of Service seem to be transparent about their use of AI partners, but if you're concerned, you might want to consider reviewing Tumblr's policies and the terms themselves.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The subprocessor list has been updated.
- Notion AI now has provisions regarding input/output ownership and default training of foundational models on customer data.
- Enterprise plans now offer additional data-residency options.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'd be happy to walk you through the changes.

One of the key changes is in the handling of **AI**. Previously, there were no specific terms related to Notion AI. However, with this update, Notion AI now has its own set of provisions.

One new provision regarding **AI** is ownership of input and output data. The Terms of Service state that, by default, Notion will retain ownership of its own output data generated using Notion AI, but it's unclear about other outputs (like inputs you sent in). 

Another new provision in the **AI** section is related to the training of foundational models on customer data. Previously, this wasn't explicitly mentioned; however, the updated Terms of Service state that Notion AI won't train its foundational models on customer data by default. However, it's worth noting that this is a default setting, so there is a possibility of this happening if changed.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service have introduced new features for **ENTERPRISE** plans, including **data-residency options**. This might be beneficial for users who require specific data storage regulations.

Lastly, there are changes to the **SUBPROCESSORS** list. This is an updated list, but the Terms of Service don't specify what kind of changes have been made.

I'm not aware of any new clauses that would harm you directly, but it's worth being mindful of the default settings regarding customer data in AI provisions.

Here are the key changes in summary:

* **AI**: New provisions regarding input/output ownership and default training of foundational models on customer data.
* **ENTERPRISE**: Additional data-residency options.
* **SUBPROCESSORS**: Updated list.
* **DEFAULT SETTINGS**: Notion AI will retain AI output data ownership by default, though specifics on client input data are unclear.

Firstly, Figma has introduced AI features, such as "Make Designs" and "Visual Search." These features allow you to leverage artificial intelligence to enhance your design experience. However, it's worth noting that you weren't notified about these features beforehand, so you may need to review how they work in detail.

Secondly, the policy has undergone changes concerning customer file content. Previously, the confidentiality language was standard, but now it's clarified that your file content won't be used to train third-party generative models without explicit opt-in. This is a positive change, as it gives you control over how your data is used.

Lastly, the updated Terms of Service also strengthen security and incident-notification language for your protection. This should provide you with greater assurance that Figma is prioritizing data security.

As for new clauses that may potentially harm you, the only significant change is the lack of prior notification for AI features. However, this change does not explicitly introduce any potential harm, so it's essential to review the specific details of these features and their usage.

That being said, if you're concerned about any aspect of the updated policy, you may want to review the AI features in more detail. Additionally, if you have any specific questions or concerns about how these changes impact you, I'd be happy to help clarify things.

- The Terms now include provisions specifically for bot developers.
- The dispute-resolution provisions have been revised.
- There are no changes to the retention periods, data collection, sharing or ownership mentioned.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over the changes in the Terms.

**Scope of the Agreement**
The Terms of Service now explicitly cover Quora and Poe, whereas previously they only covered the Quora Q&A platform. This means Poe is also subject to the Terms of Service, and you should be aware of its rules.

**Use of Poe**
A new clause has been added regarding Poe prompts and responses. The Terms of Service now explicitly state that these can be used to improve Poe and partner models, subject to your user settings. This may mean that the data you submit in Poe can be used to enhance the platform and its associated models, but only if you've allowed it through your settings.

**Bot-Developer Terms**
A new clause for bot developers has been added. This version was not present in the old Terms, and we have no details on what the new clause requires. To be safe, I recommend reviewing the section explicitly stated for bot developers to understand their obligations and responsibilities.

**Dispute Resolution**
The dispute-resolution provisions have been revised, but the details of the changes are not specified. This means that the process for resolving disputes may be different from what it was before. Be aware that the new process may impact how issues are handled and resolved.

As for clauses that may harm you specifically, we can highlight:

* The new use of Poe data, subject to your settings.
* Lack of detail on the bot-developer terms, which may carry new obligations or restrictions.

Review the updated Terms carefully to ensure you understand these changes and their potential impact on you.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Dispute resolution now involves mandated arbitration with limited class-action rights.
- You have 30 days to opt-out of the new arbitration terms, whereas previously there was no mention of an opt-out window.
- The dispute-notice window has been reduced.
- The arbitration terms now apply shortly after a data breach, whereas the old version refers to a pre-breach version.

[NARRATIVE]
According to the Terms of Service, there have been some significant changes. 

Dispute resolution is now handled through mandatory arbitration. This means that instead of going to court, any disputes will be resolved through a private process (binding arbitration).
 
To protect your rights, Class Action rights have been limited. This might affect your ability to join a class action lawsuit if a similar issue arises.

Another key change is the shortened dispute-notice window. If you have concerns, you now have a shorter time frame to let us know before a dispute arises.

Lastly, the effective date of this change coincides with the October 2023 data breach. You may want to review your account security measures in light of this new clause.

One concern here is that the change introduces a limited class-action right which might put you at a disadvantage.

To review the full changes, a 30-day opt-out window has been added for the new arbitration terms. This means you can opt-out if you don't agree with the new arbitration process within 30 days.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated. Let me walk you through the changes.

To start with, the updated Terms of Service now expand the User Content license to cover AI-generated highlights. This means that the owners of these highlights have agreed to license the content on your platform.

Another change is in the Branded Content section. The updated Terms of Service have clearer disclosure rules. While 'clearer' might be a good thing, it's worth noting that these changes aren't explicitly described as being more or less beneficial for users. I recommend reading the new rules carefully, if you create or post Branded Content.

Finally, the updated Terms of Service have updated the Arbitration procedures. Now mass-arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) is included, where one or more disputes, or a series of disputes between you and users of the platform, will be settled through the same private process.

No other meaningful changes were detected. As for new clauses that may harm you, the updated Terms of Service add coverage of AI-generated highlights, which may affect you if you post or create highlights generated artificially. Other than that, I don't see much that's explicitly detrimental.

Regarding mass-arbitration, keep in mind that this may affect you if you end up in a dispute with another user of the platform.

**Changes for you to consider:**

*  Updated User Content license - now covers AI-generated highlights
* Clarity around Branded Content disclosure rules
* Updated Arbitration procedures may be worth reading through.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Default-private accounts are now offered to under-13 users by default, whereas previously there were standard account rules.
- Parental-consent flows have been improved, while still following COPPA-style rules.
- The payout structure for creators has been revised for Robux/DevEx provisions.
- New rules have been added for Studio Assistant and avatar-creation generative-AI tools.
- The arbitration class-waiver section has been updated.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some revisions. Now, let's review the changes.

 Previously, default-standard accounts were provided to users under 13. However, that's changed. Now, users under 13 are offered **default-private accounts** (clause 1 in the current version). This change means that these users' accounts will come with a higher level of default-privacy settings by default.

The process for obtaining **parental consent** has been improved, but still follows COPPA-style rules (clause 2 in the current version).

There are changes to how **Robux/DevEx provisions** work (clause 3 in the current version), but it's not immediately clear how this will affect creators. One thing is certain, however - the **payout structure** for creators working with Robux or DevEx has been revised. The exact implications of this revision aren't immediately clear.

Regarding **AI**, the new version introduces restrictions for two tools: the **Studio Assistant** and avatar-creation generative-AI tools. You should be aware of these limitations before using these tools (clause 4 in the current version).

Lastly, the **arbitration** class-waiver section has been updated. This means that if an issue arises and you're forced to resolve it through arbitration, you won't be able to join a class-action lawsuit against Roblox (this is a private dispute process instead of court). This change may impact your potential legal recourse in certain situations.

As for new clauses that may potentially harm you - none are immediately apparent in the text. However, pay attention to how the revised **Robux/DevEx provisions** and **AI** tool limitations affect you. We recommend reviewing the changes within the Terms of Service to get a more comprehensive understanding of how these updates might impact your usage of the platform.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some significant changes. To begin with, let's address the key changes:

* Mandatory-arbitration provisions have been removed entirely. This means that you won't be required to participate in private dispute resolution through arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court).
* The class-action waiver has been removed. This gives you the right to participate in class-action lawsuits again.
* Disputes are now resolved in court, subject to applicable venue rules. This means that disagreements will be resolved by the courts, just like in any other legal situation.

As for new clauses that may harm you, it's worth noting that there are none explicitly mentioned in the updated terms as things you're being forced to do that you weren't before, with one possible concern:

* Since disputes are now resolved in court, you may be subject to court costs and fees or, in some cases, possible judgment against you, though this isn't explicitly mentioned as a new aspect introduced by this change.

Keep in mind that the updated Terms of Service aim to give you more freedom and rights, primarily focusing on dispute resolution and giving you the option to participate in class-action lawsuits.

If a third-party service causes any harm while using Uber, Uber may not be held responsible to the same extent.

Overall, these updates suggest Uber is protecting themselves from increased liability risks while also leveraging AI for improved safety features. It's always a good idea to be aware of these updates when using services like Uber.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The new Terms of Service now include "Anywhere/Icons experience terms" that were not present in the OLD version.
- The cancellation/refund policies have been revised and now also refer to "AirCover updates" which were not in the OLD version.
- The NEW version includes a new section on "automated/AI-driven listing detection" which is an anti-party tool reference not present in the OLD version.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some updates. To summarize:

When it comes to Experiences, the new guidelines include **Anywhere/Icons experience terms**, but without specifics on what these terms entail I can only report the addition.

Changes to the Cancellation policies now include **revised cancellation/refund policies** and the introduction of **AirCover updates**. What these updates mean and any implications they might have on cancellations or refunds are unclear.

Regarding AI-driven systems, the new Terms of Service **introduce a new section on automated/AI-driven listing detection**, including anti-party tools. These detection systems would help identify and prevent people from using Airbnb-hosted listings for parties or gatherings, but this new policy may be concerning if you'd like to host friends in your rental.

Lastly, there have been **updates to the arbitration provisions**. Arbitration, (a private dispute process instead of court), may become the binding method for resolving disputes, affecting how you could potentially resolve conflicts, especially in disputes related to your Airbnb-usage, especially if you host or book a listing.

These are some of the notable changes, with specific details depending on the actual content not fully outlined in this summary.

6. SUPPORT. We aim to respond to support tickets within 5 business days.

5. SUBSCRIPTION. Monthly fees are billed in advance and are non-refundable.
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate for material breach with 30 days' written notice.
7. GOVERNING LAW. These Terms are governed by the laws of Delaware.

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — X TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with X (Twitter) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Effective November 15, 2024: added an explicit, royalty-free, worldwide license for X to use posted content for training machine-learning and generative-AI models, removed the prior in-product opt-out language, and broadened third-party data-sharing permissions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by X (Twitter) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.

5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://x.com/en/tos . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240515000000*/https://twitter.com/en/tos .

user_input: Does Steam still require disputes to go to arbitration?
response: No, Steam (Valve) no longer requires disputes to be resolved through binding arbitration. The Terms of Service say that "disputes to be filed in court (subject to venue rules)" instead. This means that in the event of a dispute, you can take it to court, rather than using arbitration.

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Steam (Valve) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: September 26, 2024 update removed the mandatory arbitration / class-action waiver clauses entirely - Valve now requires disputes to be filed in court (subject to venue rules), reversing several years of arbitration-only language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Steam (Valve) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.

5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ .

user_input: Can I still get an ad-free Disney+ tier?
response: The Terms of Service say that streaming titles may now show ads even on 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers, as of January 27, 2025. This applies to new subscribers, and existing subscribers starting March 24, 2025. However, the Terms don't provide further details on how ads will be presented or which titles will have them.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — DISNEY+ SUBSCRIBER AGREEMENT (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Disney+ and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective January 27, 2025 for new subscribers and March 24, 2025 for existing ones: streaming titles may now show ads even on 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers, expanded arbitration with mass-arbitration procedures following Disney's earlier 2024 Wrongful-Death-case controversy, and updated content-availability language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Disney+ to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.disneyplus.com/legal/subscriber-agreement . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://www.disneyplus.com/legal/subscriber-agreement .

[REFERENCE ANSWER]
Under the updated Subscriber Agreement (effective January 27, 2025 for new subscribers and March 24, 2025 for existing ones), the 'no ads' / 'ad-free' tiers may now include ads on certain streaming titles at Disney's discretion. So while the tier name remains, true ad-free playback is no longer guaranteed for all content.
[MUST MENTION]
- may include ads
- no ads
- no longer guaranteed

user_input: How do I keep my right to sue 23andMe after the data breach?
response:
To keep your right to sue 23andMe, you will need to opt-out of the mandatory arbitration clause within a 30-day period. If you don't write to opt out, you will be required to arbitrate any breach-related claims in a private dispute process (binding arbitration) instead of going to court. 

Please note that you will have to take action within the specified 30-day time frame to choose between resolving disputes through arbitration or other means.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — 23ANDME TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with 23andMe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: After the October 2023 data breach, 23andMe updated its TOS to add a mandatory-arbitration clause and 30-day opt-out window, requiring users who didn't write to opt out to arbitrate any breach-related claims; also limited class-action rights and shortened the dispute-notice window.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by 23andMe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/ . The previous version is available at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/full-version/2.0/ .

Under the Terms updated after the October 2023 data breach, you are automatically opted in to mandatory arbitration unless you affirmatively opt out within the 30-day window described in the Terms by sending the company a written notice of objection. If you don't opt out, class-action rights are limited and disputes go to arbitration.
[MUST MENTION]
- mandatory arbitration
- 30-day
- opt out
- written

This will limit sharing of your public content with third parties except as necessary to operate, improve, and train Tumblr's AI/ML systems.

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Adobe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: February 2024 update added language allowing Adobe to access user content via 'automated and manual methods' to improve services and software. After backlash in June 2024, Adobe rewrote sections in clearer language, explicitly stating it does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content and added a plain-English summary of changes.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Adobe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.adobe.com/legal/terms.html . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20231101000000*/https://www.adobe.com/legal/terms.html .

user_input: Who is my contract actually with under TikTok's new Terms?
response: The Terms of Service state that the contracting party is TikTok USDS, following the US joint venture. This change occurred on January 22, 2026.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — TIKTOK TERMS OF SERVICE (US) (Effective 2026; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with TikTok and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2026 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Effective January 22, 2026: contracting party changed to TikTok USDS following the US joint venture; added explicit generative-AI rules (output 'as is', user responsibility for inputs/outputs, prohibition on stripping watermarks or claiming AI output is human-made); reaffirmed sublicensable license to use content for training ML models.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by TikTok to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.tiktok.com/legal/page/us/terms-of-service/en . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20231101000000*/https://www.tiktok.com/legal/page/us/terms-of-service/en .

Under the Terms of Service updated effective January 22, 2026, U.S. users' contracting party is TikTok USDS, the new U.S. joint-venture entity created after the divestment deal involving Oracle, Silver Lake, and MGX. Previously the contract was with TikTok Inc.
[MUST MENTION]
- TikTok USDS
- January 22, 2026

user_input: How long do I have to wait before filing arbitration against Snap?
response: The Terms of Service say that most disputes will have to go through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court). You'll have **30 days after opening your new account to opt out** of this requirement.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SNAP TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Snap (Snapchat) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective April 7, 2025: added new sections on My AI and other generative-AI features, expanded the user-content license for Live/Local/crowd-sourced services, clarified data-sharing with parents (for under-18 users via Family Center), and updated arbitration pre-dispute notice procedures.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Snap (Snapchat) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.snap.com/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://www.snap.com/terms .
ground_truth:
[REFERENCE ANSWER]
Under the updated Snap Terms (effective April 7, 2025), there is a 60-day pre-arbitration waiting period after a Pre-Arbitration Demand is sent. Arbitration may only be filed if the dispute is not resolved within those 60 days.
[MUST MENTION]
- 60-day
- Pre-Arbitration Demand
